column2: And this is held to be unconscious, abiding in nature, lord of the earth; presided over by this one, it creates and also destroys.
[Janaka said:] "These two, without beginning or end, great sage, are both formless, unmoving, unshakable and unwounded,
ungraspable, tiger among sages; how is one unconscious, and the other said to be conscious, the knower of the field?
You, best of brahmins, attend wholly on the dharma of liberation; I wish to hear the completeness of the dharma of liberation in truth:
existence and aloneness, and likewise without becoming, and the place of departure of the embodied one when parting from the body;
tell me, twice-born, the place which one gains in time, and Sankhya knowledge in truth, and yoga separately likewise.
And you ought to tell the portents of death in truth, best of the good; all this is known to you as an amalaka in the hand."
[Yajnavalkya said:] "By qualities one is endowed with qualities, and one without qualities is qualityless; so the great-souled sages who see the truth say.
The unmanifest, whose nature is of the qualities, turns to the qualities alone and uses just those; and he is ignorant by nature.
The unmanifest does not know; the Person is a knower by nature; he ever thinks, 'there is nothing beyond me.'
For this reason the unmanifest is unconscious, by being constant and imperishable, in truth otherwise than the perishable.
When through ignorance he makes the creation of qualities again and again, when he does not know the self, then he is called here the unmanifest.
From making the principles he is called possessed of the nature of principles; from making wombs he is called possessed of the nature of wombs;
from making natures he is of the nature of natures; from making seeds he is called possessed of the nature of seeds;
from the bringing forth of qualities he has the nature of bringing forth; from making dissolutions he has the nature of dissolution.
Know a gnat as one thing and a fig-tree as another; and the gnat is not stained by the fig-tree's contact.
The fish is one thing, and the water is held another; and the fish is not stained by the touch of water in any way.
Fire is one thing and the pot another; know thus always; fire is not stained by the touch of the pot.
The lotus is one thing here, and water is held another; the lotus is not stained there by the touch of water.
Their dwelling together and always their dwelling apart as it is, common folk of nature do not see constantly.
Those who see otherwise, in them right seeing is not; they enter dreadful hell, manifest, again and again.
This best vision of Sankhya has been enumerated to you; thus, having enumerated, the Sankhyas reached aloneness.
This is the illustration for others who are skilled in principle; beyond this I shall tell the vision of the yogas."
[Yajnavalkya said:] "There is no knowledge equal to Sankhya, no strength equal to yoga; both follow a single course, and both are held to be endless.
Men of small mind delight in seeing them separately; but we, king, see one alone, by settled conviction.
What the yogas see is seen by the Sankhyas too; he who sees Sankhya and yoga as one knows the truth.
Know the yogas, scourge of foes, as others with Rudra chief; with this very body they roam the ten directions.
As long as the dissolution, dear, moving through the worlds by yoga with subtle eightfold quality, giving up happiness, sinless one,
and in the Vedas, the wise call yoga eightfold; they call it subtle and eightfold, not otherwise, best of kings.
The duty of yoga is twofold, they say, the best of yogas: with quality and without, according to the illustration of the shastra.
Holding of the mind and control of breath, lord of the earth: control of breath is with quality, and holding the mind is without quality.
Having thrown off the faults of the five senses fivefold: sound, touch, form, taste and likewise smell,
and withdrawn insight and release, Maithila, having placed the whole host of senses in the mind,
and likewise the mind in ego, lord of men, ego in intellect, and intellect in nature,
having thus enumerated, he should then meditate on the alone, the dustless, stainless, constant, endless, pure, unwounded,
the Person standing as goodness, unsplittable, ageless and deathless, eternal and imperishable, the lord, Brahman imperishable.
Learn the marks of one who is joined, great king: the mark of serenity is that he sleeps happily as one satisfied.
As a lamp in a windless place burns, full of oil, with its flame motionless and upright, so the wise call one joined.
As a rock struck by drops from clouds cannot be moved, such is the mark of the joined.
With sounds of conches and drums, with varied songs and instruments being played, he does not tremble: this is the illustration of the joined.
As a man, taking a full vessel of oil in both hands, climbs a ladder, afraid and threatened by men with hands,
self-restrained from fear of them, does not let a drop fall from the vessel, so also the one ascending, with one-pointed mind,
from steadiness of the senses and from motionlessness: learn the marks of the sage so joined.
That joined one sees Brahman, the supreme imperishable, standing in the midst of great darkness, like fire.
By this he goes to aloneness, leaving the body without a witness, after a great time, king: this is the eternal scripture.
This is the yoga of the yogas; what other mark of yoga is there? Knowing it, the wise regard their work as done."
[Yajnavalkya said:] "By the shanks he would reach the Vasus and gods: so we have heard; by the knees he would reach the greatly fortunate gods and Sadhyas.
Departing by the anus he would reach the place of Mitra; by the hips the earth; by the thighs Prajapati.
By the sides the Maruts, the gods; by the nostrils the moon; by the arms Indra, they say; by the chest Rudra.
By the neck he reaches that best of sages, the unsurpassed man; by the mouth the Vishvedevas; by the ear the directions.
By the nose the carrier of scents; by the eyes the sun; by the brows the two Ashvins; by the forehead the ancestors.
By the head he reaches Brahma, the lord, the eldest of the gods. These places of departure have been told, lord of Mithila.
I shall tell the portents of death ordained by the wise, which may arise in the embodied when separation from the year is near.
He who does not see Arundhati, seen before, nor the Pole star, they say, nor the full moon, nor a lamp, who sees a broken glimmer to the south: even they have a year's life.
As a wheel with a broken nave, he sees the moon with a hole, and likewise the thousand-rayed sun: he is fit for death in seven nights.
The man who smells a dog's smell when he gets a fragrance, and who stays in a temple, is fit for death in a night.
Bowing of the ears and nose, loss of lustre of teeth and eyes, loss of consciousness and coldness are signs of immediate death.
If the left eye of a man flows suddenly, lord of men, and smoke rises from his head, it is a sign of immediate death.
Knowing these portents, the self-possessed man should join himself to the Supreme Self by night and by day.
Awaiting that time, for whatever time it is, if death is not welcome to him, he should wish to take up this practice:
he should hold all scents and tastes, collected; so he conquers death, with the inner self devoted to that.
Knowing the holding of Sankhya too, best of men, he should conquer death by yoga with the inner self devoted to that.
He would go, having reached the entire imperishable, the unborn, auspicious, undecaying, eternal, unmoving seat, hard for the unself-controlled to reach."
[Yajnavalkya said:] "By the sage's rule practised here with disrespect, the Yajus verses were obtained from the sun by me, lord of Mithila.
By great austerity I served the god, the hottest, and the lord was pleased and said to me, sinless one:
'Choose a boon, brahmana sage; I shall give you what you wish and what is hard to get; with pleased soul, for my grace is hard to get.'
Then bowing my head, I said to the best of the warm: 'I wish to know quickly the Yajus verses not yet used.'
Then the blessed one said to me: 'I shall give them to you, twice-born; Sarasvati as speech will enter your body.'
Then the blessed one said to me, 'Open your mouth,' and when I opened it Sarasvati entered.
Then, burning, I entered the water, sinless one, from ignorance and the impatience of the great-souled sun.
Then the blessed Ravi said to me, burning: 'Bear the burning a moment; then you will be cool.
You will accomplish the entire Shatapatha, best of the twice-born, and at its end you will have the thought of no rebirth.
And you will gain the state desired by Sankhya and yoga.' Having said this much, the blessed one went to his setting.
Then, hearing what was said after the god Vibhavasu had gone, I came home glad and thought of Sarasvati.
Then the goddess Sarasvati for me, most auspicious, adorned with vowels and consonants, making Om first, appeared.
Then I duly offered arghya to Sarasvati and to the best of the warm, seated, devoted to them.
Then with great joy I made the whole Shatapatha, with its collection and with its remainder, as the Sarasvati's...
Having taught a hundred best disciples, to displease the great-souled maternal uncle with his disciples,
then, with my disciples, as the sun with his rays, the sacrifice of your great-souled father was pervaded, great king.
Before Devala's eyes I took away half, and it was for my own Veda's fee, in the dispute with my uncle.
By Sumantu, Paila, Jaimini, and your father and the sages, I was then approved.
Fifteen Yajus verses were obtained by me from the sun, sinless one, and so the Purana too was grasped from Lomaharshana.
Placing this seed first and the goddess Sarasvati, and by the sun's power, I proceeded, lord of men,
to make the unprecedented Veda, the Shatapatha, and it was made by me, my purpose accomplished as desired.
It was permitted wholly to the disciples with its collection, and all the pure disciples went away very glad.
These fifteen branches, the knowledge shown by the sun, having established as I wished, I reflected on what was to be known.
'What is the Brahman-truth here, and what the unsurpassed knowable?' I was thinking there when a gandharva came and asked me.
Then, king, Vishvavasu, skilled in the knowledge of the Vedanta, having asked twenty-four questions of the Veda, lord of the earth, asked the twenty-fifth question, on logic.

All, the universe, horse and non-horse, Mitra and Varuna, knowledge, the knowable, the ignorant and the knowing, who is the warming and the not warming, the sun-eater and the sun, knowledge and ignorance,
the knowable and unknowable, king, the unmoving and the moving, the unprecedented, the imperishable, the perishable: this is the supreme question.
Then I said to him, king, to the best of gandharvas, who had asked in order the best, meaningful question:
'Bear with me a moment while I think on this.' 'Surely,' he said, and the gandharva stayed silent.
Then I thought again of the goddess Sarasvati in my mind, and that question was drawn out for me like butter from curds.
There I churned in mind the Upanishad and the remainder, lord of the earth, dear, and saw the supreme logic.
This is the fourth, tiger among kings, the knowledge of the other world; I have told you; it rests upon the twenty-fifth.
Then I said to King Vishvavasu: 'Hear what you have asked of us here.
This "all, all" which you ask, lord of gandharvas: know the all as the supreme unmanifest, terrible to past and future.
The threefold from making qualities; the childless, the partless; the horse and likewise the pair: so it is seen.
They call the unmanifest nature, and the Person without qualities; likewise Mitra is the Person and Varuna nature.
They call knowledge nature, and the knowable the partless; the ignorant and the knower, the Person; therefore he is called partless.
Who is the warmer and who the non-warmer? The warmer is said to be nature, the non-warmer the partless, the Person.
The unknowable and unmanifest, the Person is called the piercer; the moving and unmoving you said: hear that too.
They call nature moving, the cause in emission and creation; the Person is held the unmoving doer of non-emission and creation.
Both are unborn, both unproductive and both imperishable; those settled in the course of the self call both unborn and constant.
By imperishability in generation they call it unborn, imperishable; they call the Person imperishable, for he has no decay.
The wise call nature imperishable by being the doer, though by the decay of qualities; this is the fourth, the logic knowledge of the other world.
Having made wealth endowed with knowledge by action in constant action, all the Vedas are remembered as seeing one end only, Vishvavasu.
They are born and die in that, and from that they have fallen, those who do not know the meaning of the Veda, the knowable, best of gandharvas.
Even if one studies the five Vedas with limbs and subsidiaries but does not know the Veda's knowable, he is only a bearer of the Veda's load.
He who, wishing ghee, would churn an ass's milk, best of gandharvas, would see dung in it, not butter or ghee.
So he who knows the Veda's learning does not find the knowable and the unknowable; he is held only a dull-minded bearer of the load of knowledge.
These two are always to be seen with the inner self devoted to that, so that birth and death do not occur for him again and again.
Reflecting on incessant birth and death, giving up this triple Veda, resting here on imperishable dharma,
when he sees the utterly, day by day, Kashyapa, then he becomes alone and sees the twenty-sixth.
One is the ever unmanifest, another the twenty-fifth; one should see the two of him as one, say the good.
For this the yogis and the Sankhyas, seeking the highest and afraid of birth and death, do not recognise the twenty-fifth, the imperishable.'"
[Vishvavasu said:] "The twenty-fifth that you have told me, best of brahmanas: whether it is so or not so, you ought to tell.
I have heard from Jaigishavya, Asita, Devala, Parashara the brahmana sage, and the wise Varshaganya,
from the mendicant Panchashikha, Kapila, Shuka, Gautama, Arshtishena and the great-souled Garga,
from Narada, Asuri, the wise Pulastya, then Sanatkumara and the great-souled Shukra,
from Kashyapa and my father, I heard before; then from Rudra and the wise Vishvarupa,
from the gods, the ancestors and the Daityas, here and there, I received all this; they ever speak of the knowable.
Therefore I wish to hear it from your understanding, brahmana; you are the foremost of shastras, bold and exceedingly wise.
Nothing is unknown to you; you are held a treasury of scripture, and are spoken of so in the world of the gods and the world of ancestors, brahmana.
And great sages gone to the world of Brahma tell it; and the sun, lord of the warm, ever shines on you.
Sankhya knowledge, Brahmana, has been gained by you wholly, and yoga knowledge likewise, Yajnavalkya, especially.
You are free of doubt, awake, knowing the moving and unmoving; I wish to hear that knowledge, like butter from dull curds."
[Yajnavalkya said:] "I regard you, best of gandharvas, as bearing the whole; and, king, you ask me; learn it as heard.
The twenty-fifth awakens nature which does not awaken; but nature, gandharva, does not awaken the twenty-fifth.
Because of this non-awakening they call it the primary; the Sankhyas and yogis who know truth say so by the illustration of scripture.
Seeing, and not seeing, another sees, sinless one; the twenty-sixth sees the twenty-fifth and twenty-fourth; but the seer does not see, and sees him who sees him.
The twenty-fifth would think, 'there is none other beyond me'; the twenty-fourth is not to be grasped by men who see knowledge.
As a fish follows the water and proceeds by proceeding, as the fish knows, so he knows; with affection, from dwelling together, and ever with conceit.
He sinks in time when he does not awaken to oneness; he emerges from time when covered with mine-ness.
But when the twice-born thinks, 'I am another, this is another,' then he becomes alone and sees the twenty-sixth.
One is lower, king, and another is the twenty-fifth; abiding in it they see, the good say, as one alone.
For this reason the yogis and Sankhyas afraid of birth and death do not welcome the twenty-fifth, the imperishable, Kashyapa; they see the twenty-sixth, pure, devoted to that.
When he has become alone and sees the twenty-sixth, then he is all-knowing, learned, and does not find rebirth.
Thus the unawakened and the awakening, sinless one, and the awake were told in truth by me, by the illustration of scripture.
Whoever sees the seen and unseen, the safety and the truth, Kashyapa, the alone and non-alone, the primal, and what is beyond the twenty-fifth..."
[Vishvavasu said:] "True and auspicious is this you have said, rightly, safe, prior even to the gods; may good luck be yours ever, with undecaying intellect, ever joined with wisdom; honour to you."
[Yajnavalkya said:] Having said so, he went to heaven, shining with a glorious sight, and satisfied, with great joy, having done a circumambulation of me, the great soul,
to Brahma and the sky-farers and those who dwell on earth and below, lord of men; there he showed that vision, to those who have resorted to the safe path.
All the Sankhyas, devoted to the dharma of Sankhya, and likewise the yogis, devoted to the dharma of yoga, and other men who seek liberation: for them this vision of knowledge is seen.
From knowledge, liberation arises for men; not from ignorance: so they say, lord of men. Therefore knowledge is to be sought in truth, by which one frees oneself from birth and death.
Having gained knowledge from a brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya, or even a shudra or low one, one should have faith constantly; birth and death do not enter the faithful.
All classes are brahmanas and born of Brahman; all constantly speak Brahman; I say Brahman is the truth and shastra, by intellect; all this universe is Brahman.
From Brahma's mouth the brahmanas were born; from the arms the kshatriyas; from the navel the vaishyas, and from the feet the shudras; all classes are not to be known otherwise.
From ignorance they take up the womb of action, king, those and those, as they go to non-being; so classes devoid of knowledge fall, from dreadful ignorance, into the net of natural wombs.
Therefore knowledge is to be sought everywhere; this has been told to you for all places; Brahma stood, and the other who stood; to him the best of twice-born say liberation is constant.
What you asked has been taught by me as it is; be free of grief, king; go to the far shore of this matter; may good luck be yours here ever, as rightly told."
[Bhishma said:] Thus instructed by the wise Yajnavalkya, the king, lord of Mithila, was then pleased.
When the best of sages had gone and the circumambulation had been made, King Devarata, knowing liberation, sat there.
He touched ten million cows and gold, and gave a handful of jewels to the brahmanas.
And having established the kingdom of Videha for his son, the lord of Mithila lived practising the dharma of the ascetic.
Studying Sankhya knowledge and the yoga shastra wholly, king of kings, and reproaching dharma and adharma as natural,
holding it endless and the alone, constant; dharma and adharma, merit and sin, truth and untruth likewise,
birth and death, king of kings, he thought of as natural, always: 'this is the act of the unmanifest Brahman, lord of men.'

Yogis and Sankhyas see, by the marks made in their own scriptures, that Brahman, beyond the beyond, freed from the wished and unwished, stood; the learned call it constant, and pure; therefore be pure.
What is given, what one receives, what one gives and approves, and one who gives and receives, best of men, it is the unmanifest that gives this and receives it.
This was obtained by me from Janaka in the past, and by him from Yajnavalkya, king; the knowledge is excellent, not like sacrifices; one crosses the hard by knowledge, not by sacrifices.
Birth and death are hard, king; the knowers of knowledge do not speak of prosperity; by sacrifices, austerities, rules and vows, reaching heaven, they fall to earth.

Therefore attend on the supreme, great, pure, auspicious, spotless, holy liberation, the knowledge-sacrifice of the knower of the field, lord of the earth; attending on this truth you will become a sage.
Then Yajnavalkya, long ago, made the Upanishad of King Janaka: the eternal imperishable, measured, auspicious, immortal, griefless one that is reached."
[Yudhishthira said:] "By great austerity, or by action, or by learning, or by use of what elixirs does one go beyond old age and death?"
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of the mendicant Panchashikha and Janaka.
Janaka, king of Videha, asked the great sage Panchashikha, the best knower of the Veda, with his doubts of dharma and wealth cut:
'By what conduct, blessed one, may one cross old age and death: by austerity, or intellect, or action, or learning?'
Thus addressed, the knower of the unseen replied to the Videha: 'There is no turning back from these two; there is no non-turning back in any way.
Days do not turn back, nor months, nor nights; he goes on the road for long, firm, yet unfirm.
The cutting off of all beings is ever carried as by a current; carried and sinking in the raftless ocean of Time with its great crocodile of old age and death, no one gets away.
None will be his, nor is he anyone's; this is only a meeting on the road with wives and other kinsmen; no one has ever had a dwelling together for ever.
Old age and death are devourers of beings like two wolves, of the strong and the weak, the small and the great.
Among beings so, constant, yet unfirm, how should one rejoice at the born, how burn at the dead?
Whence have I come, who am I, where shall I go, whose am I, in what do I stand, where shall I be, why do you grieve?
There is no seer of heaven, nor of hell; not transgressing the traditions, one should give and sacrifice."
[Yudhishthira said:] "How does this self renounce, and how is one who has renounced his self; and what is the highest of liberation: tell me that, grandsire."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Janaka and Sulabha, Bharata.
There was once a king whose fruit was renunciation, Janaka of Mithila, known as Dharmadhvaja.
Versed in the Veda, the shastra of liberation and his own shastra, he ruled this earth with his senses collected.
Hearing of his good conduct, the wise who knew the Veda, lord of men, longed for it; other men in the worlds too.
Then in that age of dharma, practising the dharma of yoga, a lone mendicant woman named Sulabha roamed the earth.
She, wandering this world, was told of the lord of Mithila here and there in liberation by those with three staffs.
Hearing a very subtle tale, doubtful whether true or not, she resolved to see Janaka.
In the blink of an eye, fast as a light missile in flight, the fair-browed, lotus-eyed woman went to the city of the Videhas.
Reaching lovely Mithila, crowded with prosperous people, under the pretext of begging alms she saw the lord of Mithila.
The king, seeing her great delicacy and form, wondered, "Who is she, whose, or whence?" and was astonished.
Then he made her welcome, offered her an excellent seat, honoured her with water for her feet, and satisfied her with excellent food.
Then, having eaten and pleased, the mendicant spurred the king, surrounded by ministers, among the knowers of all commentaries.
Sulabha, doubtful whether he was freed in his dharmas, joined by goodness, a knower of yoga, entered his sattva with sattva, lord of the earth.
Joining the rays of her eyes with the rays of his eyes, she bound him as he was about to speak with the bonds of yoga.
Janaka the king, smiling, distinguishing her state, the best of kings received her state with his own.
Let this dialogue be heard, in one place: the freed from parasol and the like, and the freed woman with the triple staff.
Blessed lady, where has this conduct been done, and where will you go? Whose are you, or whence? the lord of the earth asked her.

In learning, in age, in birth, good being is not found; in these matters I should be told the answer at this meeting.
mahabharata:12:308.22	Know me wholly freed in the particulars such as the parasol; I wish to consult you; you ought not to be disregarded, for you are esteemed by me.
mahabharata:12:308.23	Hear also about him by whom I obtained this special knowledge long ago, of whom there is no other speaker on liberation:
mahabharata:12:308.24	I am the highly esteemed pupil of the aged, great-souled mendicant Panchashikha, of the line of Parashara.
mahabharata:12:308.25	In Sankhya knowledge and yoga, lord of the earth, and in the threefold rule of the dharma of liberation I have gone the way and cut my doubts.
mahabharata:12:308.26	Roaming here by the path seen in scripture, he once lived happily with me for the four months of the rains.
Even today the presence of Vibhavasu is at Mahishmati; it was seen by Sahadeva when he conquered the quarters then.
You alone of the gods have gained supreme heroic fortune; you ever uphold earth and sky, slayer of Bala.
Shame on me, ignorant of dharma; shame on my understanding and my learning, because of which this lord of the earth lies thus unfit.
Then he saw, from him joined in yoga, a great serpent coming forth from his mouth, white; he went toward it, being watched, by which the great-natured one reached the great ocean.
O king, greatly wise, I am pleased with you, son, by your devotion to me, by truthful speech, forbearance and self-control.
